q: Fill up: Gestational hypertension is a blood pressure of ______ mmHg or more recorded after 20 weeks in a woman without proteinuria.
exp: Gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria, and it must resolve by 12 weeks postpartum to keep the label.

q: Match the hypertensive disorder with its definition — 1) Pre-eclampsia 2) Superimposed pre-eclampsia 3) Gestational hypertension … A) New proteinuria, hypertension or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks B) Chronic hypertension with new proteinuria or a sudden worsening of control C) Hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria that settles by 12 weeks postpartum
exp: Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ involvement; superimposed disease is a change in a woman who was already hypertensive.

q: All of the following suggest impending eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Polyuria with a urine output above 200 mL per hour
Persistent frontal headache that does not respond to simple analgesia
Blurring of vision, scotomata or photophobia
Vomiting with severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
exp: Oliguria, not polyuria, accompanies severe disease; headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain are the classic warning symptoms.

q: Fill up: Eclampsia is called atypical when convulsions occur before ______ weeks of gestation or more than ______ after delivery.
opts: 20; 48 hours
28; 24 hours
20; 24 hours
34; seven days
exp: Eclampsia before 20 weeks or beyond 48 hours postpartum is atypical and should prompt a search for another cause such as a cerebral lesion.

q: Which of the following statements about posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in pre-eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: PRES causes headache, visual loss and seizures with occipital vasogenic oedema on MRI, and is managed by blood pressure control and seizure control
PRES is a haemorrhagic stroke that needs immediate neurosurgical decompression
PRES occurs only in eclampsia and is never seen in non-obstetric patients
PRES is treated with thrombolysis if the patient presents within the therapeutic window
exp: PRES is vasogenic rather than haemorrhagic, is reversible with control of pressure and seizures, and also occurs with immunosuppressants and renal disease.

q: Fill up: Trophoblast normally converts spiral arteries into ______ vessels, and in pre-eclampsia this conversion fails to reach the ______ segment.
opts: low-resistance; myometrial
high-resistance; decidual
low-resistance; decidual
high-resistance; myometrial
exp: Failed remodelling of the myometrial segment leaves high-resistance vessels, so the placenta is under-perfused and releases anti-angiogenic factors.

q: Match the mediator with its role in pre-eclampsia — 1) Excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 2) Placental growth factor 3) Endothelin-1 … A) Falls in pre-eclampsia and forms the denominator of the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio B) Antagonises VEGF and PlGF, producing endothelial dysfunction and proteinuria C) A powerful vasoconstrictor released from damaged endothelium
exp: sFlt-1 excess neutralises VEGF and PlGF, PlGF falls and endothelin rises, producing vasoconstriction, capillary leak and proteinuria.

q: All of the following are features of severe pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Haemoconcentration with a rising platelet count
Systolic blood pressure of 160 mmHg or more on two occasions
Proteinuria of 5 g or more in 24 hours
Oliguria with a serum creatinine above 1.2 mg/dL
exp: Thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration go together; a rising platelet count is not a feature of severe disease.

q: Which of the following statements about death from severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia is TRUE?
opts: Intracerebral haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death, which is why severe hypertension must be treated
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the commonest cause of death in eclampsia
Pulmonary embolism is the leading cause of maternal death in pre-eclampsia
Acute fatty liver is the usual terminal event, with profound hypoglycaemia
exp: Cerebral haemorrhage from uncontrolled hypertension kills most women with fatal eclampsia; treating severe pressure prevents it.

q: All of the following are risk factors for pre-eclampsia EXCEPT:
opts: Multiparity with a previous uncomplicated term delivery
First pregnancy or a new partner
Pre-existing hypertension, diabetes or renal disease
Family history of pre-eclampsia in the mother or a sister
exp: Previous uncomplicated pregnancy protects against pre-eclampsia; primipaternity, a new partner, medical disease and family history all raise risk.

q: Fill up: Low-dose aspirin prophylaxis is given as ______ mg daily, ideally started before ______ weeks of gestation.
exp: Aspirin 75-150 mg at night started before 16 weeks and continued to delivery reduces pre-eclampsia in women at moderate or high risk.

q: Which of the following statements about uterine artery Doppler is TRUE?
opts: Persistent early diastolic notching with a high pulsatility index at 22-24 weeks predicts pre-eclampsia and growth restriction
A diastolic notch is normal up to 34 weeks and carries no predictive value
Uterine artery Doppler is a diagnostic test that confirms the presence of pre-eclampsia
A low-resistance waveform with absent notching after 24 weeks indicates placental insufficiency
exp: Abnormal uterine artery waveform at the anomaly scan is a predictor rather than a diagnosis, and normal pregnancy loses the notch after 24 weeks.

q: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia has a blood pressure of 170/115 mmHg, 3+ proteinuria, persistent headache, platelets of 110,000 and a normal CTG. Magnesium sulfate has been started. What is the plan?
opts: Control the blood pressure, give antenatal corticosteroids, and deliver once she is stabilised
Expectant management until 37 weeks whatever the severity of the disease
Immediate caesarean section before steroids or blood pressure control
Discharge her on oral nifedipine and review her as an outpatient in one week
exp: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks means stabilise, give steroids, then deliver rather than either emergency intervention or prolonged expectancy.

q: Fill up: In fetal growth restriction, umbilical artery Doppler is the surveillance test of choice, while Doppler of the ______ detects the brain-sparing response.
opts: middle cerebral artery
uterine artery
renal artery
descending aorta
exp: Umbilical artery Doppler guides timing in growth restriction, and a reduced middle cerebral artery pulsatility index shows redistribution to the brain.

sec: Mild PE management vs severe PE management
q: Match the presentation with its management — 1) Mild pre-eclampsia at term 2) Severe pre-eclampsia before 34 weeks 3) Severe pre-eclampsia after 34 weeks … A) Delivery after stabilisation, usually within 24-48 hours B) Expectant management with steroids and magnesium in a tertiary centre C) Induction of labour and delivery, since the baby is already mature
exp: Mild disease at term is delivered; severe disease before 34 weeks may be deferred only with intensive monitoring at a tertiary centre.

sec: Severe PE & eclampsia: magnesium sulfate regimen
q: Fill up: In the Pritchard regimen the loading dose is ______ g of magnesium sulfate intravenously plus ______ g intramuscularly.
exp: Pritchard loading is 4 g intravenously and 10 g intramuscularly (5 g into each buttock), followed by 5 g intramuscularly four-hourly.
